business_problem: cure.fit needed to personalize content for different user segments while absorbing large traffic spikes across its health and wellness products without slowing feature delivery.
solution_summary: cure.fit built a microservices-based application architecture on AWS with MongoDB Atlas as the default operational database for non-relational and increasingly mainstream workloads. The team decomposed the platform into 40 microservices so features such as merchandising, offers, and user segmentation could be developed independently, then used a three-layer pattern in which the consumer app talks to an API layer that reads and writes to Atlas on the backend. Atlas became the database for more than 60% of existing microservices because its flexible document model handled varied form inputs, offer combinations, and customer-behavior data without rigid schemas, while managed operations removed the burden of backups, scaling, and observability. This let developers build personalized experiences in about an hour instead of a week, run rapid A/B tests, and keep the platform stable during pandemic-era traffic surges.

solution_components.name: MongoDB Atlas
solution_components.role: Stores segmentation, offer, and usage data for the microservices that power cure.fit's personalized app experiences.

solution_components.name: AWS
solution_components.role: Hosts the cloud-native microservices environment that connects the app, APIs, and Atlas data layer.

data_flow: User activity, form responses, offer combinations, and product-usage signals flow from cure.fit's mobile app through an API layer into MongoDB Atlas, where microservices segment users and return personalized merchandising and content experiences back to the application in real time.
business_outcome: cure.fit accelerated feature releases, improved user engagement through fast experimentation, and scaled through major demand spikes without diverting engineering effort into infrastructure management.
